        <div class="book-detail-info col-md-8 col-sm-8 col-xs-12">
            <div class="row">
                <div class="col-md-12">
                    <h1 class="book-detail-title">The Nurture of Nature</h1>

                                            <h4 class="book-detail-sub-title">Childhood, Antimodernism, and Ontario Summer Camps, 1920-55</h4>
                    
                                            <div class="book-detail-contributors">By <a href="/manon-tremblay">Sharon Wall</a></div>
                    
                                            <div class="book-detail-series">
                            <span>SERIES:</span>
                            <a href="/nature-history-society">Nature | History | Society</a>                        </div>
                    
                                            <div class="book-detail-publisher-imprint">
                            <span class="book-detail-publisher">UBC Press</span>                        </div>
                    
                    
                </div>
            </div>
								<div class="book-detail-social-share">
						<img src="/images/share.png" class="toggle-share" id="shareButton" alt="share button" />
						<div class="share" style="display: none" >
                            <div class="book-detail-social-share sharethis-inline-share-buttons" style="padding-bottom: 5.5px"></div>
						</div>
					</div>
			
                                <div class="book-detail-about-book">
                        <P>Thousands of children attended or worked at Ontario summer camps in the twentieth century. Did parents simply want a break, or were broader developments at play? <EM>The Nurture of Nature</EM> explores the history of an institution that shaped the lives of many and brings to light overlooked connections between the history of childhood, the natural environment, class cultures, and modern recreation and leisure.</P><P>Two competing cultural tendencies – antimodern nostalgia and modern enthusiasms about the landscape, child rearing, and identity – shaped the summer camp. Sharon Wall examines how this tension played out in the camp’s interaction with the natural landscape, its class and gendered dimensions, its engagement with emerging ideologies of childhood, and in the politics of race and identity inherent in its "Indian" programming. By tracing the development of summer camps in Ontario, Wall brings new insights to a broader phenomenon: the divided consciousness that has informed modern assumptions about nature, technology, and identity.</P>                    </div>
                    
                                        <div class="book-detail-promotional-headline">
                    <p><P>A nuanced discussion of the summer camp’s contribution to modern social life in North America, <EM>The Nurture of Nature</EM> is an essential resource for students and practitioners of history, sociology, and cultural studies as well as for anyone who has ever been packed off to camp and wants to explore why.</P></p>                </div>
            
            
							<h3>Awards</h3>
				<ul class="book-detail-award">
									<li>
					2010, Winner - Clio Prize (Ontario), Canadian Historical Association					</li>
									<li>
					2009, Winner - Floyd S. Chalmers Award in Ontario History, The Champlain Society					</li>
								</ul>
			
            <div class="book-detail-categories">
                                    <div class="book-detail-subjects">
                        <span>RELATED TOPICS:</span>
                        <a href="/canadian-history">Canadian History</a>, <a href="/communication-cultural-studies">Communication &amp; Media Studies</a>, <a href="/history">History</a>, <a href="/ontario-1">Ontario</a>, <a href="/race-ethnicity">Race &amp; Ethnicity</a>, <a href="/canadian-regions">Regional Studies</a>, <a href="/history-social-history">Social History</a>, <a href="/sociology">Sociology</a>                    </div>
                            </div>

            

                    </div>
    </div>

            <div class="row book-detail-tabs">
            <div class="col-md-12">
                <div role="tabpanel">
                    <ul id="book-detail-tabs-stison-block-content-2-0" class="nav nav-tabs"><li class="active"><a href="#book-detail-tabs-stison-block-content-2-0-tab0" data-toggle="tab">Reviews</a></li>
<li><a href="#book-detail-tabs-stison-block-content-2-0-tab1" data-toggle="tab">Author</a></li>
<li><a href="#book-detail-tabs-stison-block-content-2-0-tab2" data-toggle="tab">Contents</a></li></ul>
<div class="tab-content"><div id="book-detail-tabs-stison-block-content-2-0-tab0" class="tab-pane active"><blockquote  class ='review_30'>
                    <span>By seeking and revealing the cultural meanings of 'fresh air' and 'wilderness’ camping,' and of the activities in which campers engaged ... Sharon Wall has produced a multifaceted study that has much to say to historians of the environment. Time and again, <EM>The Nurture of Nature</EM> reveals the contradictory qualities of the summer camp, even as it offers new insights into the ways in which Canadians struggled to find meaning in modernity.</span>
                    <span class='footer'>
                        <span >From the Foreword by Graeme Wynn
                        </span>
                    </span>
                </blockquote><blockquote  class ='review_30'>
                    <span><EM>The Nurture of Nature</EM> represents a major study of an important but neglected subject. It is an important contribution to the study of leisure and recreation in Canada, to the understanding of the character of modernity, and to the history of summer camps.</span>
                    <span class='footer'>
                        <span >Keith Walden, Department of History, Trent University
                        </span>
                    </span>
                </blockquote></div>
<div id="book-detail-tabs-stison-block-content-2-0-tab1" class="tab-pane"><STRONG>Sharon Wall</STRONG> is an assistant professor of history at the University of Winnipeg.</div>
<div id="book-detail-tabs-stison-block-content-2-0-tab2" class="tab-pane"><P>Foreword: Modernism in Camp: A Wilderness Paradox / <EM>Graeme Wynn</EM></P><P>Introduction</P><P>1 Back to Nature: Escaping the City, Ordering the Wild</P><P>2 Socialism for the Rich: Class Formation at the Private Camp</P><P>3 "All they need is air": Building Health, Shaping Class at the Fresh Air Camp</P><P>4 Making Modern Childhood, the Natural Way: The Camp Experiment with Psychology, Mental Hygiene, and Progressive Education</P><P>5 Shaping True Natures in Nature: Camping, Gender, and Sexuality</P><P>6 Totem Poles, Tepees, and Token Traditions: "Playing Indian" at Camp</P><P>Conclusion: All Antimodern Melts into Modern?</P><P>Notes</P><P>Bibliography</P><P>Index</P></div></div>                </div>
            </div>
        </div>
